claim: The development of binocular vision is an active learning process comprising the development of disparity tuned neurons in visual cortex and the establishment of precise vergence control of the eyes.
source: The development of binocular vision is an active learning process comprising the development of disparity tuned neurons in visual cortex and the establishment of precise vergence control of the eyes.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that frames the study's focus.

claim: Under normal rearing conditions with naturalistic input, the model develops disparity tuned neurons and precise vergence control, allowing it to correctly interpret random dot stereograms.
source: Under normal rearing conditions with naturalistic input, the model develops disparity tuned neurons and precise vergence control, allowing it to correctly interpret random dot stereograms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model's performance data shown in the Results section.

claim: Under altered rearing conditions modeled after neurophysiological experiments, the model qualitatively reproduces key experimental findings on changes in binocularity and disparity tuning.
source: Under altered rearing conditions modeled after neurophysiological experiments, the model qualitatively reproduces key experimental findings on changes in binocularity and disparity tuning.
evidence: This is supported by comparisons to experimental data throughout the Results section.

claim: The model makes testable predictions regarding how altered rearing conditions impede the learning of precise vergence control.
source: Furthermore, the model makes testable predictions regarding how altered rearing conditions impede the learning of precise vergence control.
evidence: This is a prediction based on model simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The model predicts that impaired vergence control affects the statistics of orientation tuning in visual cortical neurons.
source: Finally, the model predicts a surprising new effect that impaired vergence control affects the statistics of orientation tuning in visual cortical neurons.
evidence: This prediction is supported by model simulations shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Binocular disparities are detected by populations of neurons in visual cortex that have receptive subfields in both eyes.
source: These differences are called binocular disparities and are detected by populations of neurons in visual cortex (Kandel et al., 2000; Blake and Wilson, 2011) that have receptive subfields in both eyes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established neuroscience literature.

claim: Disparity tuned neurons are frequently modeled using separate Gabor-shaped filters for each eye, where the disparity is encoded by a shift in the centers of the filters, a difference between their phases, or by a combination of both.
source: Frequently, they are modeled using separate Gabor-shaped filters for each eye, where the disparity is encoded by a shift in the centers of the filters, a difference between their phases, or by a combination of both (Fleet et al., 1996; Chen and Qian, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling literature.

claim: Vergence eye movements are learned and fine-tuned during development.
source: These so-called vergence eye movements are also learned and fine-tuned during development (Held et al., 1980; Fox et al., 1980; Stidwill and Fletcher, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: The learning of vergence control does not require any supervision from outside, but must rely on some form of self-calibration.
source: Again, this learning does not require any supervision from outside, but must rely on some form of self-calibration.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the nature of vergence learning.

claim: A critical limitation of previous studies is that they ignore the importance of behavior in shaping the statistics of the sensory input and in particular the role of vergence eye movements in determining the statistics of disparities.
source: A critical limitation of these studies is that they ignore the importance of behavior in shaping the statistics of the sensory input and in particular the role of vergence eye movements in determining the statistics of disparities.
evidence: This is a critique of prior work based on the authors' analysis of the literature.

claim: It has long been argued that the development of disparity tuning and vergence eye movements are interdependent.
source: Indeed, while it has long been argued that the development of disparity tuning and vergence eye movements are interdependent (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Candy, 2019), it has been only recently that computational models have tried to explain how the learning of disparity tuning and vergence eye movements are coupled and allow the visual system to self-calibrate (Zhao et al., 2012; Klimmasch et al., 2017; Eckmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical and recent literature.

claim: Classic efficient coding argues that sensory systems should use representations that remove redundancies from sensory signals to encode them more efficiently.
source: In a nutshell, classic efficient coding argues that sensory systems should use representations that remove redundancies from sensory signals to encode them more efficiently.
evidence: This is a description of the efficient coding hypothesis.

claim: Active Efficient Coding (AEC) extends classic efficient coding by acknowledging that developing sensory systems shape the statistics of sensory signals through their own behavior.
source: AEC goes beyond classic efficient coding by acknowledging that developing sensory systems shape the statistics of sensory signals through their own behavior.
evidence: This is a description of the AEC framework that forms the basis of the model.

claim: When the eyes are aligned on the same point, the left and right images become largely redundant.
source: For example, when the eyes are aligned on the same point, the left and right images become largely redundant.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the geometry of binocular vision.

claim: The efficient coding model can exploit redundant structure in both eyes by developing neurons tuned to small or zero disparities.
source: The efficient coding model can exploit this redundant structure in both eyes, by developing neurons tuned to small or zero disparities.
evidence: This is an inference about how efficient coding principles apply to binocular vision.

claim: Binocular neurons tuned to small disparities will represent any remaining misalignments of the eyes, providing informative input for vergence control.
source: Conversely, such binocular neurons tuned to small disparities will represent any remaining misalignments of the eyes, providing informative input for vergence control.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of disparity-tuned neurons.

claim: Learning of vergence control supports the development of neurons tuned to small disparities and this developing population of neurons in turn facilitates the learning of fine vergence control.
source: In this way, learning of vergence control supports the development of neurons tuned to small disparities and this developing population of neurons in turn facilitates the learning of fine vergence control (Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the bidirectional coupling in the AEC framework, supported by citation.

claim: Artificially inducing a strabismus (squint) leads to drastic changes in the tuning properties of neurons in visual cortex.
source: For example, artificially inducing a strabismus (squint) leads to drastic changes in the tuning properties of neurons in visual cortex (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to classic neurophysiology experiments.

claim: The model uses a virtual agent situated in a simulated environment looking at a textured plane positioned at variable distances between 0.5 m and 6 m.
source: The agent looks at a textured plane that is positioned in front of it at variable distances between 0.5 m and 6 m (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the model setup, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Planar images are used instead of a full 3D environment to allow unique definition of the correct vergence angle and ensure natural image statistics.
source: We use planar images instead of a full 3D environment to (i) allow us to uniquely define the correct vergence angle for the current visual scene and (ii) make sure that the visual input follows natural image statistics.
evidence: This explains the rationale for a design choice in the model.

claim: In the human retina, the RF size of ganglion cells increases towards the periphery.
source: In the human retina, the RF size of ganglion cells increases towards the periphery (Curcio et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a biological fact supported by citation.

claim: The model incorporates two spatial scales: a high-resolution fine scale extracted from the central part and a low-resolution coarse scale extracted from a larger area.
source: We incorporate this idea by extracting patches from an input image at two different spatial scales: A high-resolution fine scale is extracted from the central part and a low-resolution coarse scale is extracted from a larger area (orange and turquoise boxes in Figure 1 and Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the model architecture, illustrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The fine scale corresponds to the central/para-central region (including the fovea) covering a visual angle of 8.3° and the coarse scale to the near-peripheral region with a diameter of 26.6°.
source: Covering a visual angle of 8.3° in total, the fine scale corresponds to the central/para-central region (including the fovea) and the coarse scale to the near-peripheral region with a diameter of 26.6°.
evidence: This specifies the spatial extent of the two scales in the model.

claim: The two-scale architecture is more biologically plausible than using just a single scale and also increases the resulting verging performance.
source: On the one hand, this two-scale architecture is more biologically plausible than using just a single scale, on the other hand it also increases the resulting verging performance (Lonini et al., 2013).
evidence: This justifies the two-scale design with biological plausibility and performance, supported by citation.

claim: One input patch in the coarse scale can detect a disparity of up to 8.8° while one patch in the fine scale covers 1.6°.
source: One input patch (or subfield) in the coarse scale can detect a disparity of up to 8.8° while one patch in the fine scale covers 1.6°.
evidence: This specifies the disparity detection range of the two scales.

claim: The coarse scale can be used to detect large disparities, while the fine scale detects small disparities.
source: The coarse scale can therefore be used to detect large disparities, while the fine scale detects small disparities.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional roles of the two scales.

claim: Alternate rearing conditions are simulated by convolving the input images for the two eyes with two-dimensional Gaussian kernels to blur certain oriented edges, or to simulate monocular deprivation.
source: We simulate altered rearing conditions by convolving the input images for the two eyes with two-dimensional Gaussian kernels to blur certain oriented edges, or to simulate monocular deprivation.
evidence: This describes the method for simulating alternate rearing conditions.

claim: To mimic strabismus, the right eyeball is rotated inwards while the left eye remains unchanged to enforce non-overlapping input to corresponding positions of the left and right retina.
source: To mimic strabismus, the right eyeball is rotated inwards while the left eye remains unchanged to enforce non-overlapping input to corresponding positions of the left and right retina (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the method for simulating strabismus.

claim: The adaptation of the neural representation and the learning of appropriate motor commands occur simultaneously.
source: The adaptation of the neural representation and the learning of appropriate motor commands occur simultaneously: While the sparse coder updates the initially random RFs to minimize the reconstruction error, the RL agent generates vergence eye movements to minimize the reconstruction error of the sparse coder.
evidence: This describes the simultaneous learning in the model.

claim: Both the sparse coder and the reinforcement learner aim to maximize the overall coding efficiency of the model.
source: Since the sparse coder has a fixed capacity, minimizing its reconstruction error is equivalent to maximizing its coding efficiency. Thus, both the sparse coder and the reinforcement learner aim to maximize the overall coding efficiency of the model.
evidence: This explains the shared objective of the two learning components.

claim: The learning of the two components (sparse coder and RL agent) happens roughly at the same timescale.
source: The learning of the two components (sparse coder and RL agent) happens roughly at the same timescale.
evidence: This describes a property of the learning dynamics.

claim: The model is robust to variations in the learning rates, as long as the reinforcement learner's critic converges faster than the actor.
source: Our model is robust to variations in the learning rates, as long as the reinforcement learner's critic converges faster than the actor (Van Hasselt and Wiering, 2007).
evidence: This describes a robustness property of the model, supported by citation.

claim: Under normal rearing conditions the joint learning of the neural representation and motor behavior results in an agent that accurately verges the eyes on the plane in front of it.
source: Indeed, under normal rearing conditions the joint learning of the neural representation and motor behavior results in an agent that accurately verges the eyes on the plane in front of it (Klimmasch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result supported by model simulations and citation.

claim: The model obtains an accuracy of vergence eye movements of 0.12 ± 0.17° or 455.40 ± 613.75 arc sec.
source: The model obtains an accuracy of vergence eye movements of 0.12 ± 0.17° or 455.40 ± 613.75 arc sec.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model simulations.

claim: One pixel in the model corresponds to 802 arc sec, while the spacing between photoreceptors in the fovea corresponds to 28 arc sec.
source: One pixel in the model corresponds to 802 arc sec, while the spacing between photoreceptors in the fovea corresponds to 28 arc sec.
evidence: This compares the model's resolution to human visual resolution.

claim: When corrected for the model's lower visual resolution, the corrected vergence accuracy is 15.9 ± 21.44 arc sec.
source: When we correct for the model's lower visual resolution (see Materials and methods), the corrected vergence accuracy is 15.9 ± 21.44 arc sec.
evidence: This is a corrected quantitative result from model simulations.

claim: The corrected vergence accuracy falls within the range of human performance under natural viewing conditions, which is typically better than 60 arc sec (1 arc min) for stimuli not closer than 0.5 m.
source: This falls within the range of human performance under natural viewing conditions, which is typically better than 60 arc sec (1 arc min) for stimuli not closer than 0.5 m (Jaschinski, 1997; Jaschinski, 2001).
evidence: This compares the model's performance to human data, supported by citations.

claim: Random-dot stereograms (RDSs) represent the most challenging stimuli for stereopsis.
source: A second critical test of a model of the development of stereoscopic vision is whether it can handle random-dot stereograms (RDSs), which represent the most challenging stimuli for stereopsis (Lee and Olshausen, 1996; Chen and Qian, 2004; Chauhan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about RDS difficulty, supported by citations.

claim: RDSs are used in opthalmological examinations to assess stereo acuity as well as to detect malfunctions in the visual system, such as strabismus or amblyopia.
source: Nowadays, they are used in opthalmological examinations to asses stereo acuity as well as to detect malfunctions in the visual system, such as strabismus or amblyopia (Walraven, 1975; Okuda et al., 1977; Ruttum, 1988).
evidence: This describes clinical applications of RDS, supported by citations.

claim: The advantage of RDS examination is that there are no monocular depth cues (such as occlusion, relative size, or perspective).
source: The advantage of this form of examination is that there are no monocular depth cues (such as occlusion, relative size, or perspective).
evidence: This explains why RDS are useful for testing stereopsis.

claim: The impression of depth in RDS arises solely because of the brain's ability to integrate information coming from the two eyes.
source: The impression of depths arises solely because of the brain's ability to integrate information coming from the two eyes.
evidence: This explains the mechanism of depth perception in RDS.

claim: The model is able to exploit the differences in RDS images and align the eyes on the virtual plane.
source: The model is able to exploit the differences in the images and align the eyes on the virtual plane that will appear in front or behind the actual object plane in the RDS.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations on RDS.

claim: Averaged over all RDS trials, the model achieves an absolute vergence error of 0.21 ± 0.22° at the end of a fixation.
source: Averaged over all trials, the model achieves an absolute vergence error of 0.21 ± 0.22° at the end of a fixation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RDS simulations.

claim: The model's performance on RDS corresponds to a corrected vergence accuracy of 26.8 ± 28.8 arc sec.
source: This corresponds to a corrected vergence accuracy of 26.8 ± 28.8 arc sec.
evidence: This is a corrected quantitative result from RDS simulations.

claim: The model's performance on RDS is only slightly worse than its performance on natural images.
source: This is only slightly worse than the model's performance on natural images (see Figure 6) and demonstrates that the model generalizes to artificial images it has never seen before.
evidence: This compares performance across stimulus types, referencing Figure 6.

claim: When the model is trained with unaltered natural visual input, the resulting RFs resemble Gabor wavelets.
source: When the model is trained with unaltered natural visual input, the resulting RFs resemble Gabor wavelets (Daugman, 1985), as shown in the first row in Figure 2.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations, shown in Figure 2 and supported by citation.

claim: The changes that are applied to the input images in the alternate rearing conditions are reflected in the RFs that are learned.
source: The changes that are applied to the input images in the alternate rearing conditions are reflected in the RFs that are learned: Among the 10 most often selected RFs there are no vertically (horizontally) oriented RFs, when the model is trained on images that are deprived of vertical (horizontal) edges.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations under altered rearing conditions.

claim: Orthogonal RFs emerge as a result of training on orthogonal input.
source: Orthogonal RFs emerge as a result of training on orthogonal input.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: When one eye is deprived of input, the RFs will become monocular and encode information coming from the 'healthy' eye only.
source: When one eye is deprived of input, the RFs will become monocular and encode information coming from the 'healthy' eye only.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations of monocular deprivation.

claim: Strabismic rearing results in the development of monocular RFs without a preference for one or the other eye.
source: Strabismic rearing results in the development of monocular RFs without a preference for one or the other eye (Hunt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations, supported by citation.

claim: The normal case exhibits a clear over-representation of vertically (0°) and horizontally (90°) tuned RFs.
source: The normal case exhibits a clear over-representation of vertically (0°) and horizontally (90°) tuned RFs.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The over-representation of vertical and horizontal orientations has been observed in different animals and humans and is considered a neural correlate of the oblique effect.
source: This over-representation has been observed in different animals (Appelle, 1972; Li et al., 2003) and humans (Furmanski and Engel, 2000) and is considered a neural correlate of the oblique effect.
evidence: This connects the model result to biological data, supported by citations.

claim: The oblique effect describes the relative deficiency in participants' performance in perceptual tasks on oblique contours as compared to the performance on horizontal or vertical contours.
source: This phenomenon describes the relative deficiency in participants' performance in perceptual tasks on oblique contours as compared to the performance on horizontal or vertical contours (Appelle, 1972).
evidence: This defines the oblique effect, supported by citation.

claim: It has been argued that the oblique effect stems from the over-representation of vertical and horizontal edges in natural images.
source: It has been argued that it stems from the over-representation of vertical and horizontal edges in natural images (Coppola et al., 1998) and reflects the internal model of orientation distribution in the world (Girshick et al., 2011; Burge and Geisler, 2014).
evidence: This presents an explanation for the oblique effect, supported by citations.

claim: The oblique effect may reflect aspects of the imaging geometry.
source: Furthermore, it may reflect aspects of the imaging geometry (Rothkopf et al., 2009; Straub and Rothkopf, 2021).
evidence: This presents an alternative explanation for the oblique effect, supported by citations.

claim: The over-representation of vertical and horizontal orientations may be related to the rectangular pixel grid representing the input to the model.
source: Additionally, we cannot exclude the possibility that it is related to the rectangular pixel grid representing the input to our model.
evidence: This acknowledges a potential confound in the model.

claim: The distribution of orientations does not change much in the monocular and strabismic rearing case.
source: While the distribution of orientations does not change much in the monocular and strabismic rearing case, we observe a marked difference to the normal case when certain orientations are attenuated in the input.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The models trained on vertical input are missing the peak at horizontal orientations and vice versa for the horizontal case.
source: The models trained on vertical input are missing the peak at horizontal orientations and vice versa for the horizontal case.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is an increased number of neurons tuned to the dominant orientation in the input for vertical and horizontal rearing.
source: Additionally, we find an increased number of neurons tuned to the dominant orientation in the input.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observations on orientation tuning under altered rearing are consistent with animal studies.
source: These observations are consistent with animal studies (Stryker et al., 1978; Tanaka et al., 2006).
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citations.

claim: The separate analysis of the RFs in the left and right eye for the models trained on orthogonal input reveals the adaptation of each eye to its input statistics.
source: The separate analysis of the RFs in the left and right eye for the models that were trained on orthogonal input reveals the adaptation of each eye to its input statistics.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: Orthogonal RFs developed that have been observed in an orthogonal rearing study in cats.
source: Furthermore, we find that orthogonal RFs developed (also see fourth row in Figure 2) that have been observed in an orthogonal rearing study in cats (Leventhal and Hirsch, 1975).
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citation and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The models that were trained on input that is coherent between the left and right eye exhibit the majority of neurons falling in the bin with binocularity index 0.
source: The models that were trained on input that is coherent between the left and right eye (top row) exhibit the majority of neurons falling in the bin with binocularity index 0.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the normal case, more neurons fall into the binocular bin than in the vertical and horizontal case.
source: In the normal case, more neurons fall into that bin than in the vertical and horizontal case.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increased binocularity in the normal case is due to the ability of the model to perform precise vergence control.
source: This is due to the ability of the model to perform precise vergence control: Since left and right image are almost identical most of the time, the great majority of basis functions will develop to encode the exact same input from both eyes.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the binocularity result.

claim: The reduction in the number of cells with binocularity index around 0 in the vertical and horizontal rearing case is attributed to the limited vergence performance in these cases.
source: In the vertical and horizontal rearing case, we observe a reduction in the number of cells that have a binocularity index around 0. We attribute this to the limited vergence performance in these cases, that we will analyse in the next sections.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the binocularity result.

claim: If the input differs qualitatively for the two eyes, the receptive fields will also differ in their monocular sub-parts.
source: If, however, the input differs qualitatively for the two eyes (Figure 4, bottom row) the receptive fields will also differ in their monocular sub-parts.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most cells become monocular under orthogonal, monocular, and strabismic rearing, with a symmetric distribution for orthogonal and strabismic rearing.
source: Most cells become monocular, with a symmetric distribution for orthogonal and strabismic rearing.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Monocular deprivation of the right eye leads to a distribution of binocularity indices that is biased toward the left eye.
source: Monocular deprivation of the right eye leads to a distribution of binocularity indices that is biased toward the left eye.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The model's pronounced peak of binocularity indices close to 0 in the normal case matches experimental findings.
source: Comparing our model to biological data, the model's pronounced peak of bincularity indices close to 0 in the normal case matches experimental findings (Figure 1 in Wiesel and Hubel, 1963 and Figure 5 in Hubel and Wiesel, 1965).
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citations.

claim: Animals trained on inputs deprived of certain orientations develop more monocular neurons, but most neurons remain binocular.
source: Animals trained on inputs deprived of certain orientations (Figure 6B in Stryker et al., 1978) develop more monocular neurons, but most neurons remain binocular.
evidence: This cites biological data for comparison.

claim: The model's results on orientation deprivation are in good agreement with animal studies.
source: This is in good agreement with our model.
evidence: This compares model results to biological data.

claim: Kittens reared on orthogonal input show an increase in monocular neurons when compared to normal rearing.
source: Stryker et al., 1978 also reared kittens on orthogonal input and report an increase in monocular neurons (their Figure 6A) when compared to the normal rearing data from Hubel and Wiesel.
evidence: This cites biological data for comparison.

claim: In comparison to rearing on horizontal or vertical stripes, orthogonal rearing results in fewer binocular cells.
source: In comparison to the rearing on horizontal or vertical stripes, there are fewer binocular cells.
evidence: This cites biological data for comparison.

claim: The loss of binocular neurons in the model under orthogonal rearing is also reported in Hirsch and Spinelli, 1970, who reared kittens on orthogonal stripes.
source: The loss of binocular neurons that we see in our data is also reported in Hirsch and Spinelli, 1970, who reared kittens on orthogonal stripes.
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citation.

claim: Monocular rearing leads to the development of completely monocular cells after visual deprivation of the other eye.
source: Finally, monocular rearing and the analysis of binocularity was performed in Wiesel and Hubel, 1963. In their Figures 3 and 5, we see the development of completely monocular cells after visual deprivation of the other eye.
evidence: This cites biological data for comparison.

claim: The strabismic case studied in Hubel and Wiesel, 1965 revealed a division of the neural population in monocular neurons for either left or right eye, in agreement with the model.
source: The strabismic case was studied a few years later in Hubel and Wiesel, 1965 (their Figure 5A) and revealed a division of the neural population in monocular neurons for either left or right eye, in agreement with our model.
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citation.

claim: There is a noticeable difference in the number of cells that are disparity tuned between the different rearing conditions.
source: First, there is a noticeable difference in the number of cells that are disparity tuned between the different rearing conditions: In the normal case, we find the highest number of disparity tuned cells, rearing in a striped environment reduces the number, and uncorrelated input results in the smallest number of disparity tuned cells.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In every rearing condition, the distribution of preferred disparities is peaked at zero.
source: In every case, the distribution of preferred disparities is peaked at zero.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The height of the peak at zero disparity is reduced for rearing conditions with in-congruent input to the two eyes.
source: The height of this peak is reduced for rearing conditions with in-congruent input to the two eyes.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Comparing the normal with the vertical and horizontal case, there is an increase in the number of cells that are tuned to non-zero disparities.
source: Comparing the normal with the vertical and horizontal case, there is an increase in the number of cells that are tuned to non-zero disparities.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The increase in cells tuned to non-zero disparities indicates that under vertical and horizontal rearing conditions, the agents are exposed to non-zero disparities more often.
source: This indicates that under these rearing conditions, the agents are exposed to non-zero disparities more often.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the disparity tuning result.

claim: In the strabismic case, a neuron's receptive fields in left and right eye are driven by un-corresponding input, resulting in very few disparity tuned cells that exhibit a much broader distribution of preferred disparities.
source: In the strabismic case, a neuron's receptive fields in left and right eye are driven by un-corresponding input. This results in very few disparity tuned cells that exhibit a much broader distribution of preferred disparities.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fixing the strabismic angle to 3° results in an increased amount of disparity tuned cells and a shift of their preferred disparity to 3°.
source: Here, we fix the strabismic angle to 3°, which results in a corresponding image in the two eyes because one input patch in the coarse scale covers an angle of 6.4°. Figure 5—figure supplement 2 shows that this leads to an increased amount of disparity tuned cells and a shift of their preferred disparity to 3°.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The constant exposure to a certain disparity leads to a preference for that disparity for the majority of cells, exactly as in Shlaer, 1971.
source: Exactly as in Shlaer, 1971, the constant exposure to a certain disparity leads to a preference for that disparity for the majority of cells.
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citation.

claim: There has been little research on the effect of alternate rearing conditions on vergence behavior.
source: While the effect of alternate rearing conditions on receptive fields of visual cortical neurons is well studied, there has been little research on the effect of alternate rearing conditions on vergence behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The models with normal or vertical rearing learn to verge the eyes on the same point on the object, resulting in the reduction of the vergence error to small values of around 0.3°.
source: The models with normal or vertical rearing learn to verge the eyes on the same point on the object, resulting in the reduction of the vergence error to small values of around 0.3°.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The model that learns on images without vertical edges (horizontal case) also learns vergence behavior, but does not reach the accuracy of the normal and vertical models.
source: The model that learns on images without vertical edges (horizontal case) also learns vergence behavior, but does not reach the accuracy of the former models.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The orthogonally, monocularly, and strabismically reared models show only random vergence movements and do not improve throughout the training period.
source: The orthogonally, monocularly, and strabismically reared models show only random vergence movements and do not improve throughout the training period.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The only difference between the orthogonal, monocular, and strabismic models is the filtering applied to the images (the different rearing conditions).
source: Since we use the same random seeds for all simulations, including the initial weights and order of input images, the only difference between these models is the filtering applied to the images (the different rearing conditions).
evidence: This explains the experimental design.

claim: The main difference to the models that were able to learn vergence is that under orthogonal, monocular, and strabismic conditions the left and right eye are provided with incongruent input.
source: The main difference to the models that were able to learn vergence is that under these conditions the left and right eye are provided with incongruent input.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the vergence learning result.

claim: Under orthogonal, monocular, and strabismic conditions, very few neurons with disparity tuning emerge that could drive accurate vergence eye movements.
source: In these cases, very few neurons with disparity tuning emerge (compare previous section) that could drive accurate vergence eye movements.
evidence: This is an inference linking disparity tuning to vergence learning.

claim: Alterations of the visual input during a critical period of visual development lead to lasting visual deficits that can remain after visual input has been corrected.
source: In biological vision systems, alterations of the visual input during a critical period of visual development (e.g. due to astigmatism or cataract or experimentally induced alternate rearing conditions) lead to lasting visual deficits that can remain after visual input has been corrected.
evidence: This is a statement about biological vision systems.

claim: The normally trained model exhibits the best performance and achieves sub-pixel accuracy in the great majority of trials when tested after training.
source: The normally trained model exhibits the best performance and actually achieves sub-pixel accuracy in the great majority of trials.
evidence: This is a result from model testing shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The model is more accurate during testing than in the training phase, because there is no exploration noise during action selection in the testing procedure.
source: The model is more accurate here than in the training phase, because there is no exploration noise during action selection in this testing procedure.
evidence: This explains a difference between training and testing performance.

claim: Performance declines somewhat for the vertical/horizontal models, which were trained on input without horizontal/vertical edges, respectively.
source: Performance declines somewhat for the vertical/horizontal models, which were trained on input without horizontal/vertical edges, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from model testing shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Performance for the orthogonal, monocular and strabismic models is very poor when tested after training.
source: Finally, performance for the orthogonal, monocular and strabismic models is very poor.
evidence: This is a result from model testing shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The poor performance of orthogonal, monocular and strabismic models is due to their incongruent input to both eyes during training, which impairs the development of binocular neurons tuned to different disparities.
source: This is due to their incongruent input to both eyes during training, which impairs the development of binocular neurons tuned to different disparities.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the poor performance.

claim: This is the first study to investigate the quality of learned vergence movements after exposure to alternate rearing conditions.
source: Since this is the first study to investigate the quality of learned vergence movements after exposure to alternate rearing conditions (to the best of our knowledge), the differences in performance are a genuine prediction of our model.
evidence: This claims novelty for the vergence predictions.

claim: In the normal, vertical, and horizontal case, there is a pronounced minimum at zero disparity in the reward landscape, which drives the model to fixate on the same point with both eyes.
source: In the normal, vertical, and horizontal case, there is a pronounced minimum at zero disparity, which drives the model to fixate on the same point with both eyes.
evidence: This is a result from model analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the orthogonal, monocular, and strabismic conditions, the reward landscape is flat, that is, there is no incentive to align the two eyes onto the same point.
source: This is in contrast to the orthogonal, monocular, and strabismic conditions, where the reward landscape is flat, that is, there is no incentive to align the two eyes onto the same point.
evidence: This is a result from model analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Aniseikonia is a condition characterized by a perceived difference in the sizes of left and right eye images.
source: Aniseikonia is a condition characterized by a perceived difference in the sizes of left and right eye images.
evidence: This defines aniseikonia.

claim: Aniseikonia can occur naturally as result of anatomical or refraction differences of the two eyes, different spacing of photoreceptors in the retinas, or other neurological causes.
source: It can occur naturally as result of anatomical or refraction differences of the two eyes, different spacing of photoreceptors in the retinas, or other neurological causes (South et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes causes of aniseikonia, supported by citation.

claim: Aniseikonia can be induced as result of the treatment of anisometropia (different refractive powers of the eyes).
source: Aniseikonia can also be induced as result of the treatment of anisometropia (different refractive powers of the eyes) (Achiron et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes a cause of aniseikonia, supported by citation.

claim: When aniseikonia remains small (typically lower than 3%), it can be tolerated by the visual system.
source: When this difference remains small (typically lower than 3%), it can be tolerated by the visual system.
evidence: This is a statement about aniseikonia tolerance.

claim: Larger values of aniseikonia lead to problems in fusing the images and a loss of stereopsis.
source: Larger values on the other hand lead to problems in fusing the images and a loss of stereopsis (Katsumi et al., 1986; Oguchi and Mashima, 1989; Achiron et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a statement about aniseikonia effects, supported by citations.

claim: Aniseikonia may occur in anisometropic patients after cataract surgery with implanted intraocular lenses.
source: Aniseikonia may also occur in anisometropic patients after cataract surgery with implanted intraocular lenses (Katsumi et al., 1992; Gobin et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes a clinical scenario for aniseikonia, supported by citations.

claim: A recent study reported 7.8% measured aniseikonia in an outpatient clinic cohort.
source: A recent study reported 7.8% measured aniseikonia in an outpatient clinic cohort (Furr, 2019).
evidence: This cites prevalence data for aniseikonia.

claim: Little is known about the effects of aniseikonia on visual development or the potential benefits of correction.
source: Since little is known about the effects of aniseikonia on visual development or the potential benefits of correction (South et al., 2020), we conducted a series of experiments to simulate the effects of aniseikonia.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge on aniseikonia, supported by citation.

claim: Ten percent of aniseikonia leads to slower learning and a slightly reduced vergence performance.
source: Ten percent of aniseikonia leads to slower learning and a slightly reduced vergence performance.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: While an improvement in vergence performance is still present for 15% aniseikonia, it completely fails for 25%.
source: While an improvement in vergence performance is still present for 15%, it completely fails for 25%.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The increased size of the right image leads to partly incongruent input to the two eyes, resulting in an increased number of monocular RFs.
source: The increased size of the right image leads to partly incongruent input to the two eyes. As a result, an increased number of monocular RFs develops (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, see Figure 8—figure supplement 2 for a full set of RFs).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The lack of congruent input to both eyes and the resulting lack of binocular receptive fields impairs the development of correct image fusion.
source: The lack of congruent input to both eyes and the resulting lack of binocular receptive fields impairs the development of correct image fusion.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the aniseikonia effect.

claim: The different object sizes in the left and right image lead to vertical disparities.
source: The different object sizes in the left and right image also lead to vertical disparities.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of aniseikonia.

claim: The number of neurons tuned to vertical disparities initially increases with growing aniseikonia but then reduces again for 25% of aniseikonia.
source: Figure 8B shows that the number of neurons tuned to vertical disparities initially increases with growing aniseikonia but then reduces again for 25% of aniseikonia.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8B.

claim: At 25% aniseikonia, vergence behavior does not develop and many neurons assume monocular RFs, which reduces the total number of neurons tuned to vertical disparities.
source: The key to understanding this phenomenon is considering binocularity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and vergence performance (Figure 8A): at 25% aniseikonia, vergence behavior does not develop and many neurons assume monocular RFs. This reduces the total number of neurons which are tuned to vertical disparites.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the vertical disparity result.

claim: The inverted U-shaped amount of RFs tuned to vertical disparities for increasing amounts of aniseikonia is a testable prediction of the model.
source: The inverted U-shaped amount of RFs tuned to vertical disparities for increasing amounts of aniseikonia is a testable prediction of the model.
evidence: This is a prediction based on model simulations.

claim: The number of cells tuned to the vertical orientation decreases with increasing aniseikonia.
source: Interestingly, when looking at the orientation tuning in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, we observe that the number of cells tuned to the vertical orientation decreases with increasing aniseikonia (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1C for a direct comparison).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The change in orientation preference with aniseikonia is attributed to the model's (in-)ability to perform accurate vergence movements.
source: Since the distribution of orientations in the input images does not change by changing image size, we attribute this change in orientation preference to the model's (in-)ability to perform accurate vergence movements.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the orientation tuning result.

claim: The ability to detect different ranges of horizontal disparities results in an abundance of vertically tuned cells.
source: As we will elaborate in the next section, the ability to detect different ranges of horizontal disparities results in an abundance of vertically tuned cells.
evidence: This is an inference that will be elaborated in the next section.

claim: When the visual system loses the ability to detect horizontal disparities and to verge, the number of vertical RFs decreases.
source: When the visual system looses the ability to detect horizontal disparities and to verge, the number of vertical RFs decreases.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between vergence and orientation tuning.

claim: Lovasik and Szymkiw, 1985 induced aniseikonia in healthy subjects and found that the stereo acuity diminishes roughly quadratically with the level of aniseikonia.
source: Lovasik and Szymkiw, 1985 induced aniseikonia in healthy subjects and let them perform the Randot and Titmus stereo acuity tests. They found that the stereo acuity diminishes roughly quadratically with the level of aniseikonia.
evidence: This cites experimental data for comparison.

claim: The model shows that stereo acuity declines approximately quadratically with increasing aniseikonia as observed by Lovasik and Szymkiw, 1985.
source: Figure 8C shows that the stereo acuity declines approximately quadratically with increasing aniseikonia as observed by Lovasik and Szymkiw, 1985.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8C, compared to experimental data.

claim: When corrected for the model's lower visual resolution compared to humans, the stereo acuity achieved by the model falls in the typical range of human stereo acuity.
source: When we correct for the model's lower visual resolution compared to humans (see Materials and methods), we find that the stereo acuity achieved by the model falls in the typical range of human stereo acuity (Coutant and Westheimer, 1993; Bohr and Read, 2013).
evidence: This compares corrected model results to human data, supported by citations.

claim: The model appears to be somewhat more robust against larger values of aniseikonia than human subjects.
source: In fact, our model appears to be somewhat more robust against larger values of aniseikonia than human subjects (Lovasik and Szymkiw, 1985; Atchison et al., 2020).
evidence: This compares model results to human data, supported by citations.

claim: The model's greater robustness to aniseikonia is speculated to be due to the absence of an interocular suppression mechanism in the model that may accentuate the effects of aniseikonia on stereo vision in humans.
source: We speculate that this is due to the absence of an interocular suppression mechanism in our model that may accentuate the effects of aniseikonia on stereo vision in humans.
evidence: This is speculation about a difference between model and human performance.

claim: When the influence of the RL agent is removed, there is a significant decrease in the number of vertically tuned neurons.
source: When the influence of the RL agent is removed, we observe a significant decrease in the number of vertically tuned neurons.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The change in vertically tuned neurons must be caused by the different distributions of disparities that the models experience due to their different motor behavior.
source: This change must be caused by the different distributions of disparities that the models experience due to their different motor behavior, because all other parameters remain unchanged.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the orientation tuning result.

claim: In the model that was trained without disparities, there is the least amount of neurons tuned to vertical edges.
source: In the model that was trained without disparities, we find the least amount of neurons tuned to vertical edges.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The smallest number of vertically tuned cells occurs when the disparity is zero throughout the whole training.
source: We find the smallest number of vertically tuned cells when the disparity is zero throughout the whole training.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 9B.

claim: While a horizontal edge can be encoded by the same RF for all disparity values, a vertical edge demands different RFs to represent the input pattern faithfully at different disparities.
source: While the horizontal edge can be encoded by the same RF for all disparity values, the vertical edge demands three different RFs to represent the input pattern faithfully.
evidence: This is an explanation illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: A system that experiences disparities in its inputs needs to devote neural resources to represent them all.
source: A system that experiences these disparities in its inputs, needs to devote neural resources to represent them all.
evidence: This is an inference about efficient coding principles.

claim: If the distribution of disparities becomes too wide, individual neurons will receive close to independent input from both eyes and disparities that lie in the range that can be represented by a single RF will be rare.
source: If the distribution of disparities becomes too wide, however, individual neurons will receive close to independent input from both eyes and disparities that lie in the range that can be represented by a single RF will be rare.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of wide disparity distributions.

claim: The reduction of the number of vertically tuned RFs for very wide disparity distributions is explained by neurons receiving close to independent input from both eyes.
source: This explains the reduction of the number of vertically tuned RFs for very wide disparity distributions (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the orientation tuning result.

claim: Understanding the development of sensory systems requires understanding the feedback cycle between the statistics of sensory signals, neural tuning properties and behavior.
source: We argue that understanding the development of sensory systems requires understanding this feedback cycle between the statistics of sensory signals, neural tuning properties and behavior.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about sensory development.

claim: In AEC, both sensory coding and behavior are adapted to improve the system's coding efficiency.
source: In AEC, both sensory coding and behavior are adapted to improve the system's coding efficiency.
evidence: This describes the AEC framework.

claim: The coupling of perception and action is also a feature of the general framework of Active Inference.
source: This coupling of perception and action is also a feature of the general framework of Active Inference (Adams et al., 2013; Parr and Friston, 2018).
evidence: This compares AEC to Active Inference, supported by citations.

claim: In Active Inference, motor commands are generated to fulfill sensory predictions, while AEC offers a mechanism to adapt motor commands to improve sensory coding efficiency via reinforcement learning.
source: There, motor commands are generated to fulfill sensory predictions, while AEC offers a mechanism to adapt motor commands to improve sensory coding efficiency via reinforcement learning.
evidence: This contrasts AEC with Active Inference.

claim: The presented model does not make use of any efference copy of motor commands to help predict the next sensory input.
source: Interestingly, the presented model does not make use of any efference copy of motor commands to help predict the next sensory input.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model.

claim: Efference copy feedback is not required to learn accurate stereoscopic vision.
source: Evidently, such feedback is not required to learn accurate stereoscopic vision.
evidence: This is an inference from the model's success without efference copy.

claim: Extending the model to incorporate efference copies of motor commands may be interesting for calibrating pursuit eye movements.
source: However, extending our model to incorporate efference copies of motor commands may still be interesting, for example, for the case of calibrating pursuit eye movements, and is left for future work.
evidence: This is speculation about future model extensions.

claim: Both AEC and Active Inference have been linked to higher level cognitive phenomena such as imitation.
source: Interestingly, both AEC and Active Inference have also been linked to higher level cognitive phenomena such as imitation (Friston and Frith, 2015; Triesch, 2013).
evidence: This connects the frameworks to broader cognitive phenomena, supported by citations.

claim: The model has identified three critical tests that a model of the development of stereoscopic vision should pass.
source: We have identified three critical tests that a model of the development of stereoscopic vision should pass and we have demonstrated that the proposed model passes all of them.
evidence: This summarizes the model's achievements.

claim: The model autonomously self-calibrates, reaching human-like vergence performance when correcting for differences in visual resolution.
source: Specifically, we have shown that (1) our model autonomously self-calibrates, reaching human-like vergence performance when correcting for differences in visual resolution.
evidence: This summarizes a key result.

claim: The model handles random dot stereograms, despite having never been exposed to such stimuli.
source: Second, it handles random dot stereograms, despite having never been exposed to such stimuli.
evidence: This summarizes a key result.

claim: The model reproduces a wide range of findings from animal studies on alternate rearing conditions.
source: Third, the model reproduces a wide range of findings from animal studies on alternate rearing conditions, which often show dramatic effects on neural representations and behavior.
evidence: This summarizes a key result.

claim: Beyond explaining experimental findings, the model predicts systematic changes in the learned vergence behavior in response to altered rearing conditions.
source: Beyond explaining the experimental findings, our model also predicts systematic changes in the learned vergence behavior in response to altered rearing conditions.
evidence: This summarizes a key prediction.

claim: The model predicts that the learning of accurate vergence behavior systematically influences the neural representation.
source: In addition, the model predicts that the learning of accurate vergence behavior systematically influences the neural representation and offers a novel explanation for why vertical orientations tend to be over-represented in visual cortex compared to horizontal ones, at least in primates (De Valois et al., 1982b) and humans (Yacoub et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This summarizes a key prediction, supported by citations to biological data.

claim: In unilaterally enucleated animals, a bias in favor of vertical orientations over horizontal ones may be reduced or completely absent.
source: For example, in unilaterally enucleated animals, a bias in favor of vertical orientations over horizontal ones may be reduced or completely absent (Frégnac et al., 1981).
evidence: This is a testable prediction, with some support from citation.

claim: By freezing the neural network after the training period, the model simulates the state of the brain after the critical period.
source: By freezing the neural network after the training period, we also simulated the state of the brain after the critical period.
evidence: This describes a modeling approach.

claim: Even after correcting the optical aberrations present during training, a reduced vergence performance is observed for all alternate rearing regimes.
source: Even after correcting the optical aberrations present during training we observed a reduced vergence performance for all alternate rearing regimes.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: The finding of reduced vergence performance after correction is in line with evidence suggesting that optical aberrations should be corrected as early as possible to facilitate healthy development of binocular vision.
source: This finding is in line with a large body of evidence suggesting that optical aberrations should be corrected as early as possible to facilitate healthy development of binocular vision (e.g. Daw, 1998; Fawcett et al., 2005, but also see Ding and Levi, 2011).
evidence: This compares model results to clinical evidence, supported by citations.

claim: While the model's results qualitatively match experimental findings, there are some quantitative differences.
source: While our results qualitatively match experimental findings, there are some quantitative differences.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in the model's quantitative predictions.

claim: The distribution of binocularity indices and disparities in healthy animals are relatively broad, while the model finds more narrow ones.
source: In particular, while the distribution of binocularity indices (Wiesel and Hubel, 1963) and disparities (Sprague et al., 2015) in healthy animals are relatively broad (De Valois et al., 1982a; Stevenson et al., 1992; Ringach et al., 1997), we find more narrow ones in our model.
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citations.

claim: The quantitative differences are likely due to a number of simplifications present in the model.
source: These differences are likely due to a number of simplifications present in our model.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of quantitative differences.

claim: In the brain, inputs from both eyes into primary visual cortex are organized into ocular dominance bands such that individual cortical neurons may receive input which is already biased toward one or the other eye.
source: In the brain, inputs from both eyes into primary visual cortex are organized into ocular dominance bands such that individual cortical neurons may receive input which is already biased toward one or the other eye (LeVay et al., 1980; Crowley and Katz, 2000).
evidence: This describes a biological feature not present in the model, supported by citations.

claim: In the model all neurons receive similar amounts of input from both eyes and are therefore already predisposed for becoming binocular cells.
source: In contrast, in our model all neurons receive similar amounts of input from both eyes and are therefore already predisposed for becoming binocular cells.
evidence: This describes a simplification in the model.

claim: The model's narrower distribution of binocularity indices might be explained by all neurons receiving similar amounts of input from both eyes.
source: This might explain the model's narrower distribution of binocularity indices.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of a quantitative difference.

claim: Animals raised under natural conditions will experience a broad range of disparities in different parts of the visual field, since objects in different locations will be at different distances.
source: Regarding the distribution of preferred disparities, animals raised under natural conditions will experience a broad range of disparities in different parts of the visual field, since objects in different locations will be at different distances.
evidence: This is a statement about natural viewing conditions.

claim: In the model, the visual input is quite impoverished, as it is dominated by a single large frontoparallel textured plane.
source: In the model, the visual input is quite impoverished, as it is dominated by a single large frontoparallel textured plane.
evidence: This describes a simplification in the model.

claim: Once the plane is accurately fixated, most parts of the visual field will appear at close to zero disparity, which may explain the narrower distribution of preferred disparities observed in the model.
source: Once this plane is accurately fixated, most parts of the visual field will appear at close to zero disparity. This may explain the narrower distribution of preferred disparities observed in the model.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of a quantitative difference.

claim: The distribution of preferred orientations in the model shows a very strong preference for horizontal and vertical, that is accentuated in comparison to biological data.
source: Similarly, the distribution of preferred orientations in our model shows a very strong preference for horizontal and vertical, that is accentuated in comparison to biological data (Li et al., 2003; De Valois et al., 1982b).
evidence: This compares model results to biological data, supported by citations.

claim: Possible reasons for the accentuated horizontal/vertical preference include the discrete, rectangular pixel grid, the choice of image database, and the model's restriction to the central portion of the visual field.
source: Possible reasons for this include the discrete, rectangular pixel grid with which visual inputs are sampled, the choice of our image data base (Olmos and Kingdom, 2004a), which contains mostly man-made structures including buildings, etc., for which it is known that they contain an abundance of horizontal and vertical edges (Coppola et al., 1998), and the model's restriction to the central portion of the visual field, where the oblique effect is more pronounced (Rothkopf et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about the causes of a quantitative difference, supported by citations.

claim: When the main findings were repeated with a random selection of all sections from the McGill Database, the over-representation of vertical and horizontal orientations is reduced.
source: To clarify the role of the input images, we repeated the main findings with a random selection of all sections from the McGill Database (Appendix 1) and indeed found that the over-representation of vertical and horizontal orientations is reduced.
evidence: This is a result from additional model simulations.

claim: An interesting topic for future work is to use the model to study the development of amblyopia.
source: Next to addressing the above limitations, an interesting topic for future work is to use the model to study the development of amblyopia.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work.

claim: The authors have recently incorporated an interocular suppression mechanism, since suppression is considered a central mechanism in the development of amblyopia.
source: For this, we have recently incorporated an interocular suppression mechanism, since suppression is considered a central mechanism in the development of amblyopia (Eckmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes recent model extensions, supported by citation.

claim: Such models could be a useful tool for predicting the effectiveness of novel treatment methods.
source: Such models could be a useful tool for predicting the effectiveness of novel treatment methods (Papageorgiou et al., 2019; Gopal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications, supported by citations.

claim: The model highlights how stimulus statistics, sensory representation and behavior are all inter-dependent and influence one another.
source: The model highlights how stimulus statistics, sensory representation and behavior are all inter-dependent and influence one another and how alternate rearing conditions affect every aspect of this system.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's insights.

claim: The Active Efficient Coding approach may be suitable for studying various other sensory modalities across species.
source: The Active Efficient Coding approach pursued here may be suitable for studying various other sensory modalities across species.
evidence: This is speculation about the generality of the approach.
